prompt:
A logistics engineer is designing the fleet scheduling system for a warehouse with 40 autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) operating on a grid-based floor layout (50 x 30 metres, 1-metre grid cells). The robots transport totes from storage racks to 8 pick stations. Each robot has a 48 V, 20 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack with a nominal capacity of 960 Wh.

The path planning algorithm uses a time-windowed A* approach where each robot reserves a series of (cell, time_window) tuples along its planned path. When two robots' reservations conflict, the lower-priority robot replans. Priority is assigned by task urgency (time since order received). The algorithm runs on a central server with 200 ms planning cycle time.

The engineer calculates robot endurance as follows: average power consumption is 120 W (including motors, computing, and sensors), giving 960/120 = 8 hours of continuous operation. With a 15-minute fast-charge protocol that adds 50% capacity (480 Wh), the engineer schedules each robot for 4-hour work shifts followed by a 15-minute charge, achieving 93.75% uptime per robot.

The charging station has 6 charging bays, each rated at 48 V / 40 A (1.92 kW). The engineer calculates that with 40 robots on staggered 4-hour shifts, at most 10 robots need charging in any 15-minute window, and 6 bays are sufficient because the remaining 4 robots can queue for the next available bay with minimal delay.

seeded_faults.description: The priority-based replanning scheme has a deadlock vulnerability. When multiple robots of similar priority converge at an intersection or narrow corridor, each may block the other's path, and replanning cycles create livelock (repeated replanning without progress) or deadlock (circular wait on cell reservations). The time-windowed A* approach prevents head-on collisions but does not prevent circular dependencies: Robot A holds cell (5,10) and needs (5,11), Robot B holds (5,11) and needs (6,11), Robot C holds (6,11) and needs (5,10). No robot can proceed. The 200 ms planning cycle means the system detects this condition only after 200 ms, but the resolution strategy (lower priority replans) fails when all robots in the cycle have similar priority or when replanning produces a new path that creates a different deadlock. The interface fault is that the software algorithm (priority-based replanning) assumes a total ordering of priorities that always resolves conflicts, but the logistics reality (multiple robots converging at bottleneck points in a warehouse grid) creates circular dependencies that the algorithm's conflict resolution mechanism cannot break.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Priority-based replanning as the sole conflict resolution mechanism for multi-robot path planning

seeded_faults.description: The 15-minute fast-charge to 50% capacity violates LFP battery charging constraints. A 48V/20Ah LFP pack charged at 40 A (2C rate) from 50% to 100% SOC requires approximately 25-30 minutes under constant-current/constant-voltage (CC/CV) protocol, not 15 minutes. To add 480 Wh (10 Ah) in 15 minutes would require an average current of 40 A, but the CC phase can only run until the cell voltage reaches the CV threshold (typically 3.65 V/cell). For a partially-depleted LFP pack at 50% SOC, the cells are near the flat region of the voltage curve (approximately 3.3 V/cell), allowing high initial current, but the CV phase begins well before 100% SOC for LFP chemistry. Achieving 50% capacity addition in 15 minutes at 2C is physically possible for LFP (unlike NMC), but the resulting charge is closer to 35-40% than 50%, and repeated fast charging at 2C from 50% depth of discharge reduces cycle life. The cumulative effect is that the fleet's actual endurance is lower than planned, pushing more robots to the charging station more frequently and creating queuing cascades that the 6-bay station cannot absorb.
seeded_faults.location_hint: 15-minute fast charge claimed to add 50% capacity at 2C rate and the resulting charging station capacity calculation

ground_truth_notes: Software principles: Multi-agent path planning deadlock is a well-known problem (Standley 2010, Sharon et al. 2015 -- CBS algorithm). Priority-based replanning is incomplete for deadlock resolution; requires either conflict-based search with proven completeness, or explicit deadlock detection and resolution (e.g., one robot yields to a designated wait zone). Circular wait is one of the four Coffman deadlock conditions. Logistics/battery principles: LFP charging follows CC/CV protocol per cell manufacturer specifications. 2C charging of LFP is feasible but the claimed energy addition in 15 minutes exceeds what CC/CV protocol delivers due to the voltage-limited CV phase. Cycle life at 2C is reduced vs 0.5C (typically 3000 vs 5000 cycles for quality LFP cells). The interface fault (f1) is at the software-logistics boundary: the path planning algorithm's conflict resolution strategy is theoretically sound for pairwise conflicts but fails for the n-way circular dependencies that arise from the physical warehouse topology and operational patterns.
